2423367: This video lesson focuses on Environmental Safety Anchors, teaching you how to enhance your external environment with passive safety cues to support nervous system regulation. You will learn practical strategies to identify and manipulate environmental factors that promote calm and safety, laying a foundation for deeper self-regulation practices. The lesson emphasizes starting with passive cues before progressing to active engagement with the environment for improved emotional resilience.
2423372:
This lesson explores how your physical space can become a source of comfort and safety.

Your environment provides constant passive cues of safety or danger to your nervous system.

You can enhance your sense of safety through small, simple adjustments that don't cost anything.

Rearranging furniture, moving a cherished item, or tidying up can create a more comforting atmosphere.
2423380:
This lesson focuses on color as a key element in your Passive Safety Environment.

The color of a space directly signals safety or danger to your nervous system.

Natural tones like blues and greens are often cues for safety, while overwhelming colors can be jarring.

Small, inexpensive changes, like bringing in flowers or swapping a decorative object, can add pleasing colors to your space. You don't need to paint!
2423384:
Let's explore how the space around you, its tightness or openness, affects your sense of safety.

The spaciousness of a room is a passive safety cue that your nervous system constantly monitors.

Cramped or cluttered spaces can create underlying feelings of irritability and tension, even if you don't consciously notice it.

Creating more physical and visual space can help your system "breathe easier" and feel a sense of lightness and safety.
2423387:
This lesson explains why the visual tidiness of your environment is so important for your nervous system

Tidiness is about visual appeal; a clean, uncluttered space is less overwhelming for your system.

Visual clutter can be a cue for stress, while an organized space, even a full one, can feel calming and safe.

Making small changes, like clearing a surface or organizing shelves, can significantly increase your feelings of safety.
2423390:
Now - lighting

Darkness can be a natural cue for danger, often triggering feelings of anxiety or a need to be on alert.

Conversely, harsh, flickering, or overly bright lights can also feel overwhelming and unsafe.

The ideal lighting is personal and changes with your nervous system's needs; you might crave natural sunlight one moment and prefer dim, warm light the next.
2423392:
Let's explore sound and how to enhance or dampen it for your Passive Safety Environment.

The constant hum from machines in our environment is a low-level assault on our ears that creates a feeling of unease.

Our nervous systems evolved in relative silence or amidst natural noise, so reducing artificial noise can be a major cue for safety.

You can easily reduce noise intensity by adding soft items like rugs, blankets, and pillows to absorb sound and create a calmer space.
2452902:
Pick aPassive Safety Environmentthrough one of these two options:

  1. Pick the spot you want to be the safest in your home, but it is not currently.

  2. Pick the spot that is currently the safest and can be enhanced.

To identify a Passive Safety Environment through number two, follow these steps:

  1. Spend a few moments in every space in your home.

  2. Notice what levels of safety each space brings you and use one of these self-assessment options:
    (a) use the Safety Experiences download to name feelings (below)
    (b) rate each room 0-5, 5 being the safest,
    (c) ask yourself if you genuinely want to spend more time in this space.

  3. Decide which space to use.

Congrats! You’ve identified a Passive Safety Environment space in your home. We will regularly return to this space throughout the Unstucking Pathway.

2488063:
You chose a Passive Safety Environment! Woo-hoo!

Now, reflect on what about this space feels like safety to you. (This can easily change over time, so don’t get overly attached it!)

You can reflect on each of these environmental pieces if you like. One may be enough for now, as well. Listen to what you can handle and are motivated to do.

Fill in the blanks:

  • Color: [Color & object] feels like safety to me. It gives me an emotion of [safety emotion].
    - Example: “The blue walls feel like safety to me. They help me feel settled.”

  • Spaciousness: [Space description] feels like safety to me. It gives me an emotion of [safety emotion].
    - Example: “The leg room under the desk feels like safety to me. It gives me a sense of expansion.”

  • Tidiness: [Tidiness description] feels like safety to me. It gives me an emotion of [safety emotion].
    - Example: “The wicker baskets on the shelf that hold wires feel like safety to me. It gives me a sense of organization.”

  • Lighting: [Lighting description] feels like safety to me. It gives me an emotion of [safety emotion].
    - Example: “The old-timey orangish lightbulb in the desk lamp feels like safety to me. It gives me a sense of content.”

  • Sound: [Sound description] feels like safety to me. It gives me an emotion of [safety emotion].
    - Example: “The quiet of the living room feels like safety to me. It gives me a sense of calm.”

  • Positioning: [Positioning description] feels like safety to me. It gives me an emotion of [safety emotion].
    - Example: “The chair facing the window feels like safety to me. It gives me a sense of connection with the outside world.”
2452903:
Go to your chosen Passive Safety Environment. You will make one small adjustment to enhance passive safety cues.

Clean & Tidy up the obvious stuff.

The first step in your Passive Safety Environment is to clean up. After cleaning, you will incrementally work on increasing passive safety. You will also continually return to this step!

You’re not expected to do any major overhauls. Please keep it simple and focus on cleaning up obvious clutter.

Follow this list in order and do one thing at a time as you can manage it, or pick and choose from this list as you see fit:

  • wipe up any crumbs on surfaces (desk, table, etc.)

  • vacuum the floor

  • toss or file papers you don’t need out in the open

  • toss or put away stuff on the floor

  • dust surfaces

  • etc.

Take a moment.

After cleaning what you can, mindfully take in your Passive Safety Environment for ~30 seconds and reflect on the following:

  • Does this space give you a sense of like or dislike?

  • How does being in this space affect you emotionally?

  • How does being in the space affect your muscle tension?

  • Does being within this space make you more or less likely to smile?

  • create an easy seating space, like a comfy pillow on the floor with a blanket

  • position a chair facing a window

  • add a comfy pillow or blanket to your favorite seating space

2423394:
This lesson shifts our focus from the external world to your internal world, exploring how movement can be a powerful safety anchor.

Body anchors actively build on the foundation of passive safety, allowing you to exercise and strengthen your vagal brake.

Your body always has an impulse to move based on its current state; trauma can get this potential stuck in a defensive pattern.

The goal is to curiously explore movements and postures, noticing what feels safe and strengthening, not to force through discomfort.
2423395:
To help reduce the overwhelm, let's break this down into three sizes:

Large movements like running, dancing, or swimming are ideal for channeling the high energy of flight/fight states.

Medium movements, such as squeezing a fist or practicing yoga, offer a more controlled way to engage with your body's energy.

Small movements like wiggling your toes or looking around the room are subtle but powerful anchors to ground you in the present.
2423404:
Now that you know about the different body anchor sizes and their potential, let's explore the key that makes them truly effective: mindfulness.

Mindfulness is the key; without it, a safety anchor is just a fidget. Mindfully noticing sensations is what helps you climb the Polyvagal ladder.

Focus your attention on the physical experience, feel your muscles stretch, contract, and the force you exert on an object.

Let your breath do what it needs to do. Simply notice if it's flowing into your shoulders, chest, or belly as an indicator of your state.
2430286:
Now, let's put these body anchors into practice by exploring what works specifically for you.

Focus on what feels right in your body, not on perfectly identifying your specific Polyvagal state.

You are building a personalized "menu" of movement anchors by simply asking, "Does this feel right?"

Over time, you'll learn to pair the movements on your menu with specific states to help you climb the ladder.
2430287:
This lesson helps you approach body anchors with curiosity, not pressure.

Your goal isn't to force a change in your state, but to simply identify what feels safe.

There is no single "right" movement for everyone; the key is to be curious about what your unique body wants to do.

Generally, small movements help with shutdown, arm movements with fight energy, and leg movements with flight energy.
2454287:
Return to your Passive Safety Environment and try one potential body anchor. (Try more if you like.)

When you practice this potential Body Anchor in the Passive Safety Environment, reflect on the following:

  • Does it give you a sense of like or dislike?

  • How does it affect you emotionally?

  • How does it affect your muscle tension?

  • Does it make you more likely to smile?

Bonus challenge: If you found this potential Anchor to cue safety, try using it outside of the Passive Safety Environment.
2488468:
Return to your Passive Safety Environment. You will again make one small adjustment to enhance passive safety cues.

Minimize

Get rid of anything that you don't need, don't want, is clutter, or otherwise just needs to go. As Marie Kondo would recommend, if it doesn't "spark joy," then say goodbye to it! We're not tackling the entire house here, just your Passive Safety Environment. Let's significantly reduce the visual and spatial clutter and keep only what brings us joy... er, safety. It's the same thing, really.

Some ideas to minimize visually or spatially:

  • take down at least one wall-hanging

  • take down at least one object from a shelf

  • say goodbye to the books you don’t need anymore

  • intentionally organize place pillows or bedding

  • intentionally fold and place blankets that are strewn about

  • organize surface spaces (desk, table…)

  • hide exposed cords

  • tuck in chairs

Take a moment.

After minimizing, mindfully take in your Passive Safety Environment for ~30 seconds and reflect on the following:

  • Does this space give you a sense of like or dislike?

  • How does being in this space affect you emotionally?

  • How does being in the space affect your muscle tension?

  • Does being within this space make you more or less likely to smile?

2423406:
This lesson explores how you can use your five senses, taste, touch, hearing, sight, and smell, as powerful safety anchors.

Your senses constantly feed information from your environment to your brainstem, which detects cues of safety or danger.

Sensory anchors can be both passive (like the background sounds in a room) and active (like mindfully smelling a flower).

What feels anchoring is unique to you; for some, it might be the smell of citrus or the sight of a big tree.
2430624:
This lesson breaks down why some sensory cues are universal while others are deeply personal.

Some sensory cues are universally safe (like ocean waves), while others are specific to your personal history and context.

Your brain is biologically hardwired to recognize universal cues of safety and danger, a process that helped our ancestors survive.

Focus first on the senses that are most available and effective for you, building on your natural strengths to find grounding.
2423407:
Move from passively receiving sensory information to actively using it to build safety.

To build safety, you must purposefully engage your senses rather than just passively taking in information.

Mindfully noticing what safety feels like in your body creates a reference point you can return to and strengthen over time.

Slowing down is essential; it allows you to notice the small details in any sensory experience, such as textures, shadows, and colors.
2430679:
Learn how your senses connect to memory and the importance of staying in the present.

⏰ Your senses can act like a time machine, pulling you back into past moments and defensive states.

Mindfulness is your tool to stay grounded in the present, especially when a sensory experience tries to pull you into a memory.

It's essential to identify and practice your sensory anchors before a crisis, building a reference point for safety that you can access when you need it most.
2430681:
Let's turn your new awareness of sensory anchors into a simple, daily practice.

A daily sensory check-in is a practice of becoming more curious about what your senses tell you throughout the day.

The goal is to notice what feels more like a "like" versus a "dislike" in your system.

Just once or twice a day, take a moment to check in: What are you hearing, seeing, tasting, touching, and smelling?
2430680:
This is a quick, guided exercise to bring you into the present moment.

Taste & Touch: Notice any subtle tastes you're experiencing and feel the points of contact your body is making with your environment.

Hearing: Tune into the sounds around you, both near and far, setting my voice aside for a moment.

Sight: Look around and notice the colors, shapes, and light in your immediate space.

Smell: Finally, take a moment to see what scents you can detect in the air.

2423408:
Learn to use music as a safety anchor.

Music is a uniquely powerful safety anchor that deserves its own lesson, separate from the other senses.

Music works in two ways: as a passive cue you simply hear in the background, or as an active anchor you mindfully listen to.

You can combine music with movement by mindfully dancing, blending it with your body anchors.
2423409:
Here's a look at prosody, the "secret ingredient" that makes music a powerful anchor for safety.

Vocal prosody is the sing-song quality of a voice, and it's a direct indicator that someone is in their safety state.

Hearing prosody in another person's voice sends a powerful safety cue to your own nervous system, a process called co-regulation.

Music with a rich vocal range provides these same co-regulatory cues, which is why some singers can make us feel so calm and connected.

Beyond the voice, the instruments themselves have a musical prosody that sends your system cues of either safety or danger
2430745:
Let's explore how different kinds of music connect with your internal states.

Certain songs or genres naturally align with your current Polyvagal state, making you feel deeply understood.

The feeling and rhythm of the music are more important than the lyrics; they connect directly to your nervous system.

Music can help you climb your ladder by mindfully connecting with your current state or by gently nudging you one rung up.

A great first step is to create a "safety playlist" with songs that consistently feel good to your system.
2430751:
Now, let's try a simple exercise to see how music affects you right now.

Play a random piece of music from the radio or a smart device.

The first step is to simply notice your body's immediate "like" or "dislike" reaction.

Consider if the music matches your current state or feels like it's a step up the Polyvagal ladder.

Pay attention to whether the music helps you feel more grounded and safe, or less so.

2423414:
This lesson introduces a different way to work with your thoughts, moving away from a struggle and toward a new strategy.

While thoughts are often the most noticeable part of our inner experience, they are also incredibly difficult to control directly.

Trying to fight, combat, or shut off your thoughts usually backfires, creating more frustration and making you feel stuck.

The goal of cognitive anchoring isn't to battle your thoughts, but to gently and proactively guide your awareness instead.
